lesson.title: Naming the fallacies

lead.text: Start with the neighbour's rule: “If it rains, the street gets wet.” In the words of the if-then lesson, rain is the antecedent, the part after “if”, and a wet street is the consequent, the part after “then”. With p for rain and q for a wet street, the rule is p → q.

The rule is a promise about what rain does. Whenever p is true, q has to be true, so if you learn that it is raining you may safely say the street is getting wet. The arrow runs from rain to wet street. It tells you what follows from rain, and it says nothing about what else might make a street wet, such as a street cleaner or a burst pipe.
So there are two directions to travel along a rule, and the arrow only vouches for one of them. The next question puts the neighbour's step to that test.
Back at the gate: the rule says that rain wets streets, and the street is wet.

The neighbour went against the arrow. A wet street is the consequent, and having found it true, the neighbour concluded that the antecedent was true as well, that it rained. Reasoning that looks as if it works and doesn't is called a fallacy. This one has a name of its own, affirming the consequent, because the second premise asserts, or affirms, the consequent.

Test the pattern the way the last lesson taught, by hunting for a counterexample, a case in which both premises hold and the conclusion fails. A street cleaner supplies one. The rule is true and the street is wet, yet it did not rain. The premises hold and the conclusion is false, so the pattern can lead from truth to falsehood, which makes it invalid.
In letters the pattern is “p → q; q; therefore p”. It treats p → q as though it said q → p, and the lesson on converses showed that those are two different claims.
In letters, p is “It rains” and q is “The street is wet”, so the neighbour's reasoning is “p → q; q; therefore p”.

reveal.text: Compare your choice with the street cleaner's case: the street is wet and it never rained. The premises hold, and the conclusion doesn't.

lead.text: The rule has a second trap. Suppose the morning is dry and someone says, “It didn't rain, so the street is dry.” This time the argument starts from the antecedent being false and concludes that the consequent is false as well. It is called denying the antecedent, because the second premise denies p. The conclusion is ¬q.

The mistake is the same one in a different place. The rule says what happens if it rains. It is silent about what happens if it doesn't, so it leaves the street free to be wet for another reason. The street cleaner serves again: it did not rain, the street is wet and the rule is never broken. The pattern “p → q; ¬p; therefore ¬q” has a counterexample too.

The two slips mirror each other. One goes from a true consequent back to the antecedent, and the other from a false antecedent forward to a false consequent. Each treats the rule as though it ran in both directions.
Now the second pattern, in the case of the street cleaner: no rain, but a wet street.

Not every way of using a rule goes wrong. Suppose it is dry outside and you want to know whether it rained. The rule says that rain would have left the street wet, and the street is dry. So it did not rain, and you can say so with no doubt at all.

The reason is that the rule promises a wet street if it rained. Suppose it had rained: then the street would be wet, and it isn't. That supposition contradicts what we see, so it has to be rejected. This also moves against the arrow, from the consequent back to the antecedent, but it starts from a false consequent, where the slip started from a true one.

The pattern is “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p”, and it is called modus tollens, Latin for the mode that denies. It is valid, and it is the contrapositive from the earlier lesson at work, since ¬q → ¬p says exactly what the original rule says.

steps.headline: “If the sensor overheats, the light turns on. The light is off.” What follows?

lead.text: A new rule, with the same move.

workedSteps.math: Then the light would be on

workedSteps.text: But the light is off, which contradicts that.
This pattern is valid. It is called modus tollens.

lead.text: Now the same pattern in letters. Keep only the rows where p → q and ¬q are both true.

steps.headline: Answering the argument, not the person

lead.text: The slips so far are about the shape of the reasoning. There is another kind of slip that has nothing to do with shape, and it is answering the speaker instead of the argument. Suppose someone says, “Their sum must be wrong because they are rude.” Whether a person is rude and whether a sum is right are two separate matters, and the first gives no evidence about the second.

This is called attacking the person. It works in the flattering direction too: “Everyone admires her, so her sum must be right.” In both cases the speaker's manner, popularity or record is treated as though it were a reason. A reason that bears on the conclusion has to be about the sum itself.

To answer an argument, find the step you doubt and test it. You can recheck a calculation, look for a missing premise or search for a counterexample, as we did with the patterns above. If the argument holds up, it holds up whoever says it.
Someone has been dismissed in a discussion for being rude. Choose the reply that deals with what they said.

lesson.orientation: Name two invalid patterns of if-then reasoning and the valid one beside them.
lesson.nextAction: Try the changed cases in your review queue.

blocks.text: On a grey morning you step outside and find the street wet. A neighbour at the gate says, “If it rains, the street gets wet. The street is wet. So it rained.” It sounds like a tidy bit of reasoning, and most people would nod.

It sounds right, and yet a doubt nags. The street might have been wet for a different reason, and if so the neighbour's rule has been pushed further than it goes. Reasoning of this kind is common because it looks exactly like reasoning that works. The way to catch it is to know the shapes by name.

This lesson names two slips that people make with an if-then rule, and the one safe move that sits beside them. It finishes with a slip of another kind, which is answering the speaker in place of the argument.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name two invalid ways of reasoning from an if-then claim, and tell them from a valid one.

recap.keyIdea: Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid, but modus tollens is valid. Answer the reasoning, not the person.

blocks.text: You found that a street cleaner defeats both slips: p false and q true keeps the premises true and makes the conclusion wrong. A light that stays off showed that a sensor never overheated, and a rude speaker turned out to tell you nothing about the sum.

recap.nextHook: That is the last lesson in this course. The changed cases in your review queue are the best way to keep these patterns fresh.

questions.prompt: Which case refutes “p → q; q; therefore p”?
hints: Both premises must stay true, so keep p → q true and q true.
To refute the conclusion p, make p false.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With p false and q true both premises hold and the conclusion p fails.

questions.onCorrect: p false, q true: both premises hold and p is false. A true consequent doesn't establish its antecedent.

misconceptions.feedback: Here p is true, so the conclusion holds. You need a case where it fails.
Here q is false, so a premise fails. Keep both premises true.

questions.prompt: Take p false and q true in “p → q; ¬p; therefore ¬q”. Is the conclusion ¬q true or false?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conclusion ¬q is false because q is true.

questions.onCorrect: False. Both premises hold but ¬q fails, so denying the antecedent is invalid.

misconceptions.feedback: The conclusion is ¬q, and q is true here. What does negation do to it?

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p” valid or invalid?
hints: Suppose p were true while q is false.
Would that satisfy the first premise p → q?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both premises force p false, so ¬p follows.

questions.onCorrect: Valid. If p were true, p → q would force q, but ¬q says otherwise. This is modus tollens.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where p → q and ¬q are true and ¬p is false. Is there one?

questions.prompt: Someone argues, “Their calculation must be wrong because they are rude.” Which response examines the reasoning?
hints: Rudeness says nothing about the sums.
Choose the response that looks at the step or the evidence.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Checking the disputed step addresses the reasoning. Manners don't settle it.

choices.label: Treat the speaker's popularity as proof

questions.onCorrect: Check the step itself. Rudeness doesn't make a calculation right or wrong.

misconceptions.feedback: That attacks the person again. It doesn't test the calculation.
Popularity is not evidence about the calculation either.

questions.prompt: In “p → q; q; therefore p”, which part is affirmed: antecedent or consequent?
hints: In p → q, p comes before the arrow and q after it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: q is the consequent, which the argument affirms.

questions.onCorrect: Consequent. The argument asserts q, the part after the arrow.

misconceptions.feedback: The antecedent is p, before the arrow. Which letter does the second premise assert?

questions.prompt: In “p → q; ¬p; therefore ¬q”, which part is denied: antecedent or consequent?
hints: Which part of p → q does p stand for?
The second premise ¬p denies that part.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p is the antecedent, which the argument denies.

questions.onCorrect: Antecedent. ¬p denies p, the part before the arrow.

misconceptions.feedback: The consequent is q. The second premise denies p. Which part is that?

questions.prompt: Does the street being wet prove that it rained? Answer yes or no.
hints: The rule says what rain does. Does it say rain is the only way?
Could a street be wet for another reason?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. Something else could have wet the street.

questions.onCorrect: No. The rule says rain wets the street. It doesn't say nothing else does.

misconceptions.feedback: Rain is one way to get a wet street. Does the rule say it is the only way?

questions.prompt: “If the sensor overheats, the light turns on. The light is on, so the sensor overheated.” Which part of the conditional is affirmed: antecedent or consequent?
hints: The antecedent follows “if”, and the consequent follows “then”.
Which part does the second sentence assert?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The light being on is the consequent.

questions.onCorrect: Consequent. The argument asserts the “then” part and argues back to the “if” part.

misconceptions.feedback: The antecedent is the “if” part, the overheating. The second sentence asserts the light being on.

questions.prompt: Why does the light being off show the sensor didn't overheat?
hints: Suppose it had overheated. What would the rule say about the light?

acceptedIdeas: Overheating would have turned the light on, and it didn't.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If it had overheated, the light would be on. It isn't, so it didn't.

questions.onCorrect: Overheating would have turned the light on. It is off, so the sensor didn't overheat.

choices.label: Overheating would have turned the light on, and it didn't.
The light is only on when nothing overheats.
Sensors that don't overheat keep their lights off.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the rule. It says what overheating does to the light.
The rule doesn't say that. It says what overheating does, not what happens without it.

questions.prompt: “If it's a bird, it has feathers. This animal has feathers, so it's a bird.” Is this reasoning valid or invalid?
hints: Which part of the rule does the second sentence assert?
Is there a way to have the feathers without being a bird?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Other animals could have feathers too. It affirms the consequent.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid. It affirms the consequent: feathers could come from another source, so the rule doesn't give the conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule says what birds have. Does it say only birds have feathers?
